strengths: The proposed SDDLM loss (Equation 7) is a genuinely simple and well-motivated simplification of the complex ELBO-derived USDM objective, restricting the denoising loss to noise-replaced tokens in analogy with masked diffusion models; the intuition for why the naive reconstruction loss fails (Equation 6) is clearly articulated.

Substantial empirical effort: models trained on LM1B and OWT at 170M for 1M steps, plus a scale-up to 1.1B parameters on SlimPajama, with multiple baselines (Duo, SEDD-Uniform, UDLM, PLAID), multiple evaluation axes (Gen PPL, entropy, ELBO-based PPL, zero-shot transfer PPL, eight QA benchmarks), and few-step sampling comparisons (Figure 3).

Concrete efficiency gains are demonstrated (Figure 2): reduced peak GPU memory (53GB to 40GB) and lower wall-clock training time while maintaining comparable generation quality, which directly supports the scalability claim.

The contrastive-learning interpretation of the negative-gradient regularizer (Section 4.3, Equation 10) is a nice conceptual framing that connects discrete diffusion training to self-supervised learning and suggests future directions.

Reproducibility is reasonably supported: full hyperparameter tables for both model scales (Tables 5-6), Algorithm 1, dataset/evaluation details in the appendix, generation samples with reported perplexity/entropy, and a code link.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core contribution is essentially cross-entropy on corrupted positions (predicting x0 given xt), which is a standard simplification also used in discrete flow matching (Gat et al., 2024); the regularizer is a uniformity-avoidance term closely related to existing contrastive/uniformity objectives. No theoretical analysis (e.g., relation of the simplified loss to the true likelihood or ELBO, conditions under which it is valid) is provided.

The central 'comparable performance' claim rests heavily on GPT-2-Large generative perplexity and sequence entropy, which are known to be imperfect proxies for generation quality; no human evaluation or stronger task-based generation metrics are provided. Moreover, ELBO-based likelihood measurably degrades (Figures 4, Section 5.3), and the paper argues the mismatch 'may not affect' true likelihood without directly verifying this claim.

A key baseline (the naive reconstruction objective, Equation 6) is excluded from all comparisons due to 'unstable convergence,' and the epsilon-stabilization ablation for SDDLM-V1 is also omitted, leaving important design choices empirically unsubstantiated.

Large-scale results are mixed rather than clearly favorable: on the eight QA benchmarks (Table 4), SDDLM-V1 is broadly comparable to Duo with some wins and losses (e.g., BoolQ 59.66 vs 60.55), and zero-shot PPL on WikiText is slightly worse (35.02 vs 33.91). Absolute scores are low overall, and only a single scale jump (170M to 1.1B) is shown, so the scaling claim is weakly evidenced (no scaling-law fit, no seeds/variance reporting).
The SDDLM-V1 entropy consistently decreases relative to Duo/SDDLM (Table 2, Figure 5), indicating a diversity loss trade-off that is acknowledged only superficially and not analyzed.

Presentation quality is below standard for the venue: multiple typos ('simpilfied varaint', 'denosing noisiy', 'Lanuage', 'indicating indicating'), inconsistent figure references (text cites Figure 5 for results shown in Figure 1), and awkward phrasing throughout.
The efficiency comparison (Figure 2) may partly conflate loss simplicity with other Duo components (curriculum, distillation machinery); the source of the training-time savings is not decomposed.

strengths: The core idea is simple and sensible: restricting the denoising loss to noise-replaced tokens for uniform-state diffusion LMs stabilizes training while cutting computational cost (13→15 vs 17h training time, 40 vs 53GB memory in Fig. 2).

The paper is honest about a real tension: SDDLM does not optimize the ELBO, so ELBO-based perplexity worsens even as Gen PPL improves, and it discusses this mismatch rather than hiding it (Section 5.3).

Experiments cover two scales (170M and 1.1B), multiple datasets (LM1B, OWT, SlimPajama) and a set of zero-shot QA benchmarks, plus a few-step sampling comparison (Fig. 3), which is more than a minimal evaluation.
The hyperparameter details, training algorithms, dataset descriptions, and qualitative generation samples are provided in the appendix, which supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central claims are only weakly supported. 'Comparable performance to the complex ELBO loss' holds for Gen PPL, but Table 3 shows SDDLM is worse than Duo on Wikitext (35.02 vs 33.91) and Lambada (51.50 vs 51.29), and Table 4 shows mixed results at 1.1B (Duo better on BoolQ, RACE; SDDLM-V1 better on ARC-e, LAMBADA). The headline efficiency gain in Fig. 2 (~15% wall-clock, ~25% memory) is modest for the claimed scalability contribution.

A critical ablation is missing: the ε-constant added to pθ is acknowledged as essential ('training of SDDLM without adding ε will directly lead to break'), yet no sensitivity analysis or value of ε is reported. Since the whole negative-gradient mechanism depends on this unstudied constant, the evidence for SDDLM-V1 is incomplete.

The regularizer explicitly sharpens output distributions, which directly lowers GPT-2 Gen PPL while also reducing entropy (5.31/5.33 vs 5.55 for Duo, Table 2). Reduced diversity could mechanically improve Gen PPL without genuinely better generation; the paper does not disentangle this confound.

The contrastive-learning connection (Section 4.3) is interpretive rather than substantive: the 'negative gradient' is just a uniform-distribution push-away term (Eq. 10), and the promised 'more principled negative sampling strategies' are deferred to future work, so SDDLM-V2 (using xt as negatives) is the only actual variant and yields no clear gain.

Claims about the naive baseline (Eq. 6) causing 'training collapse' cannot be verified because that baseline is excluded from all comparisons, and no learning curves or failure analysis are shown for it.
No error bars, seeds, or statistical significance for any result; several benchmark differences (e.g., Table 4 within ~0.5-1 point) are likely within noise.

Presentation quality is poor for a main-track submission: multiple typos ('simpilfied varaint', 'denosing noisiy', 'indicating indicating', 'Diffusion Lanuage'), Table 1 appears before its section and duplicates Table 7, figures are referenced out of order, and Equation 4/5 are dense and hard to parse.

The framing that prior USDM losses 'hinder scalability' is asserted but never demonstrated: no scaling-law experiments, no compute-matched Pareto analysis, and the largest model is only 1.1B, so the 'strong potential for large-scale training' claim remains speculative.
Duo itself is a concurrent arXiv preprint, so the significance of beating/tie-ing it is hard to assess, and the retrained Duo numbers introduce reproduction risk.

strengths: The core contribution is practical and well-motivated: replacing the complex ELBO-derived USDM loss (Eq. 4) with a simple selective denoising cross-entropy (Eq. 7) plus a negative-gradient regularizer is a clean, easily adoptable idea, and the efficiency gains are concretely demonstrated (Fig. 2: 40GB vs 53GB peak memory and reduced wall-clock training time at comparable quality).

Experiments are reasonably thorough for this class of work: 170M models trained for 1M steps on LM1B and OWT, scaling to 1.1B models on SlimPajama, evaluation across generation quality (Gen PPL, entropy), ELBO-based likelihood, zero-shot perplexity on 5 datasets (Table 3), 8 QA/next-word benchmarks at 1.1B scale (Table 4), and CFG variants (Tables 1, 7).

The paper is transparent about an interesting and potentially valuable negative result: ELBO-based perplexity increases while generation quality improves substantially (Sec. 5.3, 6), highlighting a mismatch between likelihood-based evaluation and sample quality in USDMs. The contrastive-learning interpretation of the negative gradients (Sec. 4.3) is a reasonable conceptual framing.

The anti-uniform sharpening regularizer consistently improves Gen PPL across sampling-step counts (Fig. 3) and improves next-word prediction (LAMBADA: 31.75 vs 17.02 for Duo at 1.1B), suggesting the effect is real rather than noise.
Hyperparameters for both small and large models are provided in the appendix, and the method follows existing setups (Duo, Nie et al.) to enable fair comparison.
weaknesses: Originality is modest. The base objective (Eq. 6) is acknowledged to come from discrete flow matching (Gat et al., 2024), and restricting the loss to corrupted tokens mirrors the masked-diffusion recipe. The main novelty reduces to (i) applying this recipe to uniform-state diffusion and (ii) a negative-sampling/KL-style regularizer, whose relation to existing negative-contrastive/negative-sampling objectives is not analyzed.

The empirical claims rest on a comparison where the key baseline is missing: the naive reconstruction loss (Eq. 6) is excluded 'due to unstable convergence' with no curves, seeds, or diagnosis provided, weakening the causal story for why selective denoising is necessary.

There is little theoretical grounding. No derivation connects the simplified loss to the ELBO (even approximately), no analysis of the bias introduced by ignoring unchanged positions, and the claimed ELBO-vs-quality mismatch is observed but not explained. The epsilon-stabilization of the negative gradient (Sec. 4.2) is ad hoc, and the statement that training without it 'will directly lead to break' is asserted without the ablation the authors say was omitted.

The entropy metric is presented as a diversity indicator (higher is better), yet the best-performing method (SDDLM-V1) has lower entropy than Duo (4.10 vs 4.20; 5.31 vs 5.55). This tension between diversity and the claimed quality gains is never confronted, and Gen PPL via GPT-2 Large is a proxy metric with known biases; no human or alternative-quality evaluation is provided.

Results at scale are mixed rather than clearly superior: on zero-shot PPL (Table 3) SDDLM is slightly worse than Duo on Wikitext and AG News, and on the 1.1B benchmark suite (Table 4) SDDLM-V1 wins on some tasks and loses on others (e.g., BoolQ 59.66 vs 60.55). The 'comparable' framing is defensible but the headline claims ('strong potential for large-scale training') somewhat overstate what two scales and one large dataset establish.

Presentation quality detracts from the work: repeated typos and duplicated phrases ('simpilfied varaint', 'indicating indicating', 'Preplexity'), a placeholder code link ('this link'), broken/awkwardly formatted equations (Eq. 5), inconsistent figure cross-references (Fig. 1 vs Fig. 5), and a somewhat disorganized related-work section.

Reproducibility is currently incomplete: the code link is not functional in the manuscript, and details such as the number of evaluation seeds, the exact Gen PPL sampling protocol, and the curriculum-learning schedule referenced in Appendix C.4 are underspecified.
